title: Quinn Emanuel Vet Launches AI-Powered Firm For High-Stakes Cases (Chris Kercher / Kercher Law)
pub: Original Jurisdiction (David Lat Substack; interview built around Kercher's first-person account)
author: Christopher Kercher · David Lat

dom.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source recognises that automating junior-intensive context assembly will affect staffing, training and billing, but it does not develop the cluster’s central concern that automation may undermine expertise reproduction or propose deliberate replacement training. Instead, it reframes the issue around building an AI-integrated litigation firm that redesigns roles and workflows while preserving human advocacy.
qs: This shift has profound implications for the architecture of a law firm: how matters are staffed, how work flows, how young lawyers are trained, and how clients are billed.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source frames AI as a driver of AI-native boutique formation and a potential “force multiplier,” but provides no evidence about multidisciplinary implementation, substantive verification, task-specific evaluation or reliable service outcomes. The excerpt therefore neither clearly accepts nor rejects the cluster’s implementation-focused proposition.
qs: But partners are also leaving, drawn by AI’s potential to be what Cravath partner turned boutique founder Benjamin Gruenstein [called](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/business-and-practice/cravath-partner-gruenstein-launches-boutique-firm-in-new-york) a “force multiplier.”[1](#footnote-1)  The latest leading litigator to depart from a storied firm is Chris Kercher.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: Kercher accepts that AI-assisted production can disrupt traditional staffing, workflow, training and billing, and extends the cluster by proposing a concrete first-principles response: build a new litigation firm that allocates work among associates, paralegals and AI while preserving lawyers’ counselling and advocacy roles. The account is a practice-design thesis, not evidence of measured outcomes.
qs: What is the right role for an associate, for a paralegal, for software or AI?”  “When you’re in a system and you’re in a process, that is the system, that is the process, and it’s difficult to reinvent from first principles,” he said.
This shift has profound implications for the architecture of a law firm: how matters are staffed, how work flows, how young lawyers are trained, and how clients are billed.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Kercher accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI will automate document-heavy production while durable human advocacy, judgment and dispute resolution remain valuable. He materially extends it with a concrete operating model: redesign staffing and workflows from first principles and use phased fixed fees to transfer more pricing risk from clients to the AI-enabled firm.
qs: Today, AI can handle much of this context assembly, such as document review or due diligence.

“I’m leaning hard into ‘fixed fee by phase’ billing, so clients can always understand the cost to get to the next level—while also knowing that they can always step off the treadmill at any time.”  Fixed-fee billing—whether by phase or by matter, which Kercher said he’s also open to discussing—limits the client’s risk (which is why clients like it), while exposing the firm to more risk.

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI value depends on redesigning legal delivery, then concretely develops it through a blank-slate litigation firm integrating AI into staffing, workflows, junior training and billing. It also adds an iterative pricing mechanism: fixed-fee losses can generate data for improving future prices, while human courtroom advocacy remains central.
qs: This shift has profound implications for the architecture of a law firm: how matters are staffed, how work flows, how young lawyers are trained, and how clients are billed.

But he also acknowledged that there might be cases where a firm takes a financial hit because of a fixed-fee arrangement—where a firm might “get punched in the face,” as he put it (paraphrasing Mike Tyson)—and smart firms will learn from those experiences, using that data to improve their pricing for future cases.

st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that AI adoption implicates practice design and pricing rather than productivity alone. Kercher’s independent AI-driven practice and iterative fixed-fee pricing illustrate business-model adaptation, while Wingens predicts that lower costs may expand demand. The support is largely experiential and predictive, not measured evidence of productivity, revenue or demand effects.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central claim that AI is changing legal practice without eliminating lawyers, emphasizing enduring human functions in advice, strategy and negotiation. Its discussion of AI-enabled independent practice, fixed-fee experimentation and possible demand expansion also aligns with workflow and commercial reconfiguration, though it provides little evidence on verification or competence risks.
qs: “It’s the same job, in many ways, that Abraham Lincoln probably had: Clients come in with a problem, you advise them, you counsel them, you strategize, maybe you negotiate.”
The long version rests on certain timeless aspects of law and the legal profession—which make Kercher confident that lawyers aren’t going anywhere.

He argues that clients will continue to need human advice, strategy and negotiation, although the source provides interview-based reasoning rather than workforce evidence and does not assess the specific risk to junior pipelines.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source endorses the cluster’s principal proposition that AI requires operating-model redesign rather than simple tool adoption. Kercher proposes rebuilding staffing, workflows and delivery from first principles while retaining lawyers’ courtroom advocacy, and he acknowledges that resulting changes to training and billing involve practical trade-offs rather than automatic gains.
qs: And in Kercher’s view, building a new firm from the bottom up is the best way to integrate AI into every aspect of running a law firm and serving one’s clients.
This shift has profound implications for the architecture of a law firm: how matters are staffed, how work flows, how young lawyers are trained, and how clients are billed.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: Kercher supports the cluster’s overall view that AI will be absorbed into ordinary legal practice, automate selected tasks and alter monetisation without eliminating legal demand. He also reinforces the cluster’s expectation that advocacy, negotiation and contextual human judgment will remain durable sources of value. The source does not materially address organisational readiness, verification or measured adoption outcomes.
qs: Noting that the practice of law is one of civilization’s most enduring professions, he predicted that “it’s never going away, because it’s how we mediate conflict.”  AI might eliminate certain tasks—or, to be more precise, the ability of lawyers to make money from performing those tasks.

kp.k: AI motivates departures and experimentation outside established firms
kp.d: Lat reports that Chris Kercher left Quinn Emanuel after more than 17 years to launch Kercher Law, principally to explore AI’s potential. Kercher argues that established processes constrain reinvention and that founding a firm lets him determine the appropriate mix of associates, paralegals and software from first principles. This is a practitioner account of organisational experimentation, not evidence of an established optimal staffing model.
qs: The short version of his answer can be summed up in a word: AI.
What is the right role for an associate, for a paralegal, for software or AI?
Launching my own firm presented the rare opportunity to start with a blank slate, with something brand-new and unconstrained.

kp.k: AI shifts context assembly away from expensive lawyer labour
kp.d: Kercher characterises much historical legal expenditure as assembling documents, facts, memoranda and research. The article asserts that AI can now perform much of this work, including document review and due diligence, with implications for staffing, workflows, junior training and billing. It does not supply measured productivity results or a specific replacement training model.
qs: you had all these documents, all these facts, all these memos, all this legal research
Today, AI can handle much of this context assembly, such as document review or due diligence.
This shift has profound implications for the architecture of a law firm: how matters are staffed, how work flows, how young lawyers are trained, and how clients are billed.

kp.k: Electrification analogy supports integrated rather than incremental redesign
kp.d: Kercher invokes factory electrification and Henry Ford’s Highland Park plant as an analogy for embedding AI throughout a new firm rather than attaching tools to existing processes. The historical comparison expresses his design rationale, not empirical evidence that his firm’s model outperforms established firms.
qs: If you look at electrification and early industrial work, factory owners would take their factories and add a light bulb here, a motor there
What if we build electricity throughout the factory? What if we just assume that electricity exists, so we can get its benefit in everything we do?
And that’s how I’m looking at building, from day one, the systems to bring this all together.

kp.k: Phase-based fixed fees transfer pricing risk toward firms
kp.d: Kercher says he is adopting fixed fees by litigation phase and is open to matter-level fixed fees. His rationale is that hourly billing protected firms against unexpectedly labour-intensive matters, whereas cheaper AI-based context assembly makes assuming more cost risk feasible. Clients gain visibility into the cost of the next phase and the option to stop; the claimed reduction in firm risk is not quantified.
qs: has been largely de-risked
I’m leaning hard into ‘fixed fee by phase’ billing, so clients can always understand the cost to get to the next level—while also knowing that they can always step off the treadmill at any time.
can be handled by compute, rather than associates.

kp.k: Fixed fees retain exceptions and potential financial losses
kp.d: Lat reports Kercher’s qualification that fixed-fee contracts may permit additional billing in truly exceptional circumstances, and that some matters can still cause financial losses. Kercher expects firms to use experience from such losses to improve subsequent pricing; AI is therefore not presented as eliminating pricing risk entirely.
qs: even a fixed-fee arrangement might include provisions allowing the firm to bill more than originally anticipated in truly exceptional or extreme situations.
smart firms will learn from those experiences, using that data to improve their pricing for future cases.

kp.k: Lower costs and predictability may expand litigation demand
kp.d: The article proposes that capped, more predictable costs could make clients more willing to litigate, offsetting some work lost to AI. Separately, it quotes Lowenstein Sandler chair Gary Wingens predicting that cheaper work will activate previously deferred or abandoned matters. These are demand-expansion predictions, not observed market outcomes or evidence about unmet civil legal need.
qs: This could make clients *more* willing to litigate, based on the greater predictability about what it might cost—in turn generating more work for firms.
As work becomes faster and cheaper, clients will buy more of it, not less.
In practice, that means matters that clients once deferred, narrowed, or abandoned can suddenly become economically viable and move from a client’s ‘nice to have’ bucket to the active docket.

kp.k: Human advocacy remains central despite AI-assisted intermediate work
kp.d: Kercher frames AI primarily as augmentation: clients still require counselling, strategy, negotiation and courtroom advocacy even when they have access to Claude or ChatGPT. He regards persuasive advocacy, negotiation and board presentations as especially protected human activities. This is his assessment of professional resilience, not a measured finding about displacement.
qs: Where does a human fit in? Clients have Claude; clients have ChatGPT. Why are they coming to lawyers?
And much of that work in the middle, between the client coming in and advocating for the client in court, can be assisted and augmented by AI.
The most protected part in law is that endpoint: the person who’s doing the advocacy, conducting the negotiation, presenting to the board.

kp.k: Tool adoption becomes ordinary litigation rather than separate practice
kp.d: Lat reports Kercher’s public discussion of using Claude for strategy and Syllo AI for document review. Kercher rejects a lasting distinction between AI-native litigation and litigation generally, describing technology as a means to extend lawyers’ capabilities. The article references these uses without presenting comparative performance data.
qs: Kercher has spoken publicly about using specific, cutting-edge tools to litigate cases, such as Claude to [strategize](https://law-disrupted.fm/ai-system-built-by-litigators-2/) and Syllo AI to [review](https://law-disrupted.fm/winning-at-trial-with-ai/) documents.
It’s not ‘AI-native litigation,’ but litigation with an understanding of how we can use AI and technology more generally to get more out of our work and to really extend ourselves.

kp.k: Enduring disputes underpin optimism despite uncertain occupational transition
kp.d: Kercher predicts that legal services will not decline as a percentage of GDP and that the profession will persist because people need institutions and advocates to mediate conflict. The article distinguishes eliminating tasks or revenue from particular tasks from eliminating underlying client needs. Kercher explicitly leaves the transition and future shape of work unresolved, without a numerical forecast or specified horizon.
qs: If you think about legal as a percentage of GDP, I really don’t think it goes down
What the transition to the future looks like, including the shape of the work, is an open question.
AI might eliminate certain tasks—or, to be more precise, the ability of lawyers to make money from performing those tasks.
What’s left? What’s left is human disputes. Human disputes are not going anywhere.

kp.k: Established firms also pursue substantial litigation AI investment
kp.d: In a closing note, Lat reports a partnership between Syllo and Kirkland & Ellis and Kirkland’s plan to invest $500 million in AI over the next three to four years. This is a reported investment plan, not completed expenditure or demonstrated returns; Lat’s favourable assessment of a 2024 Syllo demonstration is a personal impression rather than an evaluation study.
qs: I saw a demo of Syllo AI back in 2024, and I was blown away
which plans to invest [$500 million](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/business-and-practice/kirkland-ellis-investing-500-million-to-build-ai-platform) in AI over the next three to four years.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Kercher predicts that AI will reduce the human work and cost of litigation preparation, enable redesigned firms and fixed-fee billing, and augment rather than eliminate lawyers; Lat describes a possible resulting increase in demand.
pts.d: Kercher argues that AI can assist much of the work between a client's initial consultation and courtroom advocacy. Lat's account of Kercher's position identifies document review and due diligence as examples of 'context assembly' that AI can now handle substantially, with consequences for staffing, workflows, junior training and billing. Kercher says founding a firm from scratch allows more thorough integration than modifying established processes. He is adopting fixed fees by phase because, in his account, AI reduces the cost and uncertainty of additional preparation work, making it more feasible for the firm to bear cost-overrun risk. Lat suggests that greater cost predictability could encourage clients to litigate and generate additional work. Kercher predicts that legal services will not decline as a share of GDP, although the future shape of work remains uncertain. He regards advocacy, negotiation and board-level presentation as especially protected human functions and expects the profession to endure because disputes persist. The article distinguishes the loss of tasks or revenue from those tasks from the elimination of underlying client needs.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal basis is Kercher's practitioner experience and first-person reasoning, supplemented by examples of tools and adoption rather than quantitative outcome evidence.
pts.d: The article grounds Kercher's claims in approximately 25 years of legal practice, more than 17 years at Quinn Emanuel, three years exploring AI applications, his founding of Quinn Emanuel's AI and Data Analytics Group, and teaching at Stanford and NYU. It reports his public discussion of Claude for strategy and Syllo AI for document review. His new firm's design and planned pricing provide examples of decisions motivated by these beliefs, not demonstrated financial results. His factory-electrification analogy supports the argument for integrated redesign. Lat adds his favorable impression of a 2024 Syllo demonstration and reports Kirkland & Ellis's Syllo partnership and planned AI investment as adoption context. The supplied text does not report measured cost savings, accuracy results, staffing changes, fixed-fee profitability or demand increases. The expectations about demand, legal spending and occupational durability are arguments and predictions rather than quantified findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: AI-assisted preparation and firm redesign are presented as current opportunities in the 2026 account; market expansion and the profession's survival are open-ended forecasts with explicit qualifications.
pts.d: Kercher presents the reduction of context-assembly risk and his shift to phase-based fixed fees as present developments. His broader career framing looks ahead 25 years, but the source gives no specific date for market-wide transformation or its legal-spending prediction. The fixed-fee argument depends on additional work being manageable through compute rather than additional associates. Exceptional situations may permit extra billing, and firms may still lose money and need to use experience to improve pricing. Protection against replacement is particularly qualified by lawyers' ability to persuade judges and juries and perform other client-facing advocacy. Kercher explicitly leaves the transition and future composition of work unresolved. His expectation that AI use will simply become part of litigation has no specified adoption deadline.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate focus is high-stakes commercial litigation, its clients, boutique founders and established firms, with different implications for preparatory work and senior advocacy.
pts.d: Clients are expected to gain more predictable phase costs and opportunities to stop before incurring further expense. Firms accepting fixed fees take on more downside risk, which Kercher expects AI to make more manageable. Boutiques can design systems around AI from inception, whereas established firms face constraints from existing processes. Associates and paralegals face reconsideration of their roles as AI performs more context assembly; junior training is identified as affected, but the source does not specify a headcount reduction or replacement staffing model. Lawyers performing advocacy, negotiation and board presentations are described as especially protected. Lat's potential demand expansion concerns clients making more litigation economically attractive, not a demonstrated reduction in the civil justice gap. The profession-wide spending and survival predictions extend beyond the immediate commercial-litigation setting.
